extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (prosecutors, attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of patent applications under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) — written description, enablement, and best mode — including special considerations for computer‑implemented functional claims and interaction with 35 U.S.C. 103(c) joint-research disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR applies across technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's KSR principles are not limited to 'predictable' arts; KSR applies across technologies and Office personnel should not withdraw a rejection solely because the invention lies in a technological area ordinarily considered unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat biotechnology or other 'unpredictable' arts as exempt from the KSR obviousness framework; consider predictability as a factor but apply KSR principles generally (citing In re Kubin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom supports nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom in the art may be evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Hedges — process claimed at temperatures above accepted optimum indicated contrary-to-accepted-wisdom and supported nonobviousness. Consider whether claimed approach runs counter to known teachings suggesting a different course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known disadvantages in prior art may support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Known disadvantages in old devices which would naturally discourage search for new inventions may be taken into account when determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether prior art contains discouraging teachings or recognized disadvantages that would have deterred a skilled artisan from pursuing the claimed invention (citing United States v. Adams).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) joint research agreement disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) shall not preclude patentability under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, as demonstrated by three conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three requirements to disqualify commonly-assigned prior art (joint research agreement disqualification): (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Applies only to prior art under 102(e),(f),(g) relied upon in a rejection under 103; does not disqualify prior art relied on for anticipation under 102. Be mindful of statutory amendments and effective dates (1999 AIPA, 2004 CREATE Act) when assessing applicability in reexamination and pending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must include three distinct requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must include (A) a written description of the invention, (B) the manner and process of making and using the invention (enablement), and (C) the best mode contemplated by the inventor — and these three requirements are separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate written description, enablement, and best mode; analyze each independently when examining an application (citing statute and case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must be understandable to a person of ordinary skill and demonstrate actual possession as of the filing date. Generic or purely boundary-defining language may be insufficient to support a claimed genus; claims described only in functional terms may fail if the specification does not identify how the invention achieves the claimed function. The required level of detail varies with claim scope and the complexity/predictability of the technology. Original claims may or may not satisfy the requirement depending on the disclosure. See Ariad, Vas-Cath, LizardTech examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description for computer-implemented functional claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions claimed functionally, the specification must disclose both sufficient hardware and sufficient software (algorithms/steps) so that one skilled in the art reasonably concludes the inventor possessed the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses the computer type and the necessary steps/algorithms (e.g., in sufficient detail to program a microprocessor), written description may be satisfied (In re Hayes). Conversely, purely functional recitation without disclosure of how the function is achieved (hardware plus algorithm/steps/flowcharts) may support a 112, para. 1 rejection. Examiners should determine whether the spec discloses the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps/flowcharts) to perform the claimed function in sufficient detail for a person skilled in the art to program the computer to perform those steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Wands factors to determine undue experimentation (see separate Wands entry). The enablement inquiry is case-specific and fact-intensive. The scope of the claims must be supported by an enabling disclosure commensurate with the claim scope; broad functional claims raise concerns about whether the disclosure enables the full scope. If a reasonable basis exists to question enablement, the examiner must articulate reasons and applicant must rebut with facts/demonstration. Examples (Sitrick, Auto. Techs., ALZA) show that inability to enable novel aspects or to extend teachings across distinct media (video games vs movies) can render claims non-enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wands factors for undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when determining whether undue experimentation is required to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The In re Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of ordinary skill in the art; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; and (8) quantity of experimentation necessary to make or use the invention based on the disclosure. Weigh all factors — there is no single dispositive factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claims must be commensurate with the scope of enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of enablement provided by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that enables only a subset of claim scope cannot support broader claims. Example: Sitrick where specification enabled integration into video games but not movies; claims covering both were not enabled. Ensure applicants provide sufficient teachings for all media/embodiments covered by claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on general skill in the art to supply novel enabling details
rubrics_metrics.description: While known information in the art may be omitted from the specification, an applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information necessary to enable the novel aspects of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must supply the novel aspects; omission of minor details may be acceptable, but where no disclosure of specific starting materials or process conditions exists for the novel aspect, enablement may fail (citing Genentech, ALZA, Auto. Techs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (general and software-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best mode requires a subjective determination whether the inventor knew a best mode at the time of filing and an objective determination whether that best mode was disclosed in sufficient detail to allow one skilled in the art to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For software-containing best modes, disclosure of the functions of the software typically satisfies best mode because writing code is ordinarily within the skill of the art; flowcharts or source code listings are not required. Evaluation of best mode focuses on whether disclosure quality suggests concealment of a preferred embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural guidance for examiners (guidelines status and burdens)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP guidelines are Office policy to assist examiners but do not constitute substantive rulemaking; rejections must be based on substantive law and supported by the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where examiners establish a prima facie case of lack of written description or enablement, a thorough review of prior art and other statutory requirements must be conducted prior to completing an Office action. Examiners must articulate a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy of disclosure; once done, applicant must rebut with factual demonstration. Per the MPEP, perceived failure to follow these Guidelines is not appealable or petitionable.
